answers.answer: Redis is an in-memory key-value database and data structure server. It keeps keys and typed values such as strings, lists, and sorted sets primarily in RAM, with optional disk persistence. Its low-latency use cases include caching, user sessions, job and priority queues, pub/sub and streams, and secondary indexing, text search, and vector similarity search.

RDB periodically saves a point-in-time snapshot of the whole dataset, using a forked child so the parent can keep serving. A failure can lose writes since the last snapshot, potentially minutes depending on save points. The AOF records writes for replay. Its durability depends on the sync policy, with everysec risking about one second of writes. If both are enabled, startup restores from the AOF because it offers better durability.
The background I/O service, the jobs it handles, and its ordering guarantee are not stated. The artifact separately describes optional socket I/O threads and background snapshots in a forked child.

The modules API lets shared libraries extend the server with commands and data types. The artifact describes loading a library at startup with a loadmodule configuration directive. How to load into an already running server and how a module saves and restores its own types are not stated.

The ae event loop waits for file descriptors to become ready and dispatches their handlers. On a ready listening TCP socket, the connection handler accepts the socket and passes it to acceptCommonHandler, which creates the client and installs readQueryFromClient. On a readable client socket, that callback fills the query buffer, and the networking code parses and dispatches complete commands for checks and execution. Replies are buffered. Before the next wait, beforeSleep flushes the AOF when enabled and sends pending replies. serverCron also checks snapshot save points. The full order of timer processing within a turn is not stated.

The in-memory keyspace maps binary-safe string keys to typed values. In cluster mode, keys are divided over 16,384 hash slots. The key and expiration containers, how those containers change in cluster mode, and how a key's name is physically stored relative to its value are not stated.

A type is the kind of value exposed to the client, such as a string, list, set, hash, or sorted set. The artifact mentions compact hashes as an internal representation that shares field names among keys with the same schema. A general definition of encoding, why Redis maintains both classifications, and who chooses the encoding are not stated.

The artifact identifies src/cluster.h for hash slot mapping and src/cluster_legacy.c in connection with cluster-bus internals. The full division of clustering responsibilities is not stated. CRC16 of the key name maps the key to one of 16,384 slots. During command checks the server redirects keys owned by another node, and multi-key commands require keys to share a slot. The exact slot calculation and special routing cases are not stated.

The socket read callback fills a query buffer, and processInputBuffer parses inline or multibulk input. A complete command reaches processCommand, which looks up the command, checks ACL permissions, can redirect keys belonging to another node, applies the memory limit through eviction, and refuses writes on a persistence error. If no key can be evicted, commands needing memory can fail. Inside MULTI it queues the command. Otherwise, call runs the handler and addReply buffers the reply. Writes are propagated via alsoPropagate and propagateNow to the AOF buffer when enabled and to replicas. beforeSleep flushes the AOF before sending buffered replies. appendfsync controls when the log is synced to disk, and replica delivery is asynchronous.

The multipart AOF has a base snapshot and incremental command files, ordered by a manifest. New propagated writes are put into an in-memory AOF buffer and flushed in beforeSleep. How a rewrite starts, which file receives writes during it, and how the new base and manifest are installed and old files retired are not stated.

The replica connects with SYNC or PSYNC, handled by syncCommand. For a short disconnect, if the master's backlog still holds the missing writes, partial resync sends those writes so the replica catches up. Full resync copies the dataset again. Exact eligibility checks and the sequence for a full transfer are not stated.

The artifact mentions expiration as a feature for cached keys. The removal mechanisms, how the active expiration work limits its cost, and how expiration is propagated to replicas and the AOF are not stated.

The artifact says eviction policies including LRU use randomized approximations. Why the project chose approximation over exact LRU, how it samples and ranks victims, and the costs or accuracy of the approximation are not stated.

The reasons and costs of incremental hash-table resizing, and the reasons and costs of discouraging resizing while a background child is running, are not stated. The artifact describes the snapshot child and the parent continuing to serve.

The manifesto favors a simple, efficient mostly single-threaded core and scaling through separate shared-nothing instances, which suit NUMA. A slow command holds up the other clients of its instance. Optional I/O threads offload socket reads, parsing, and writes. They are off by default, recommended only for a real performance issue on a machine with at least four cores, and unsupported for TLS connections. Background saves use a forked child process. Other uses of threads and their costs are not stated.

appendfsync controls the trade-off between sync overhead and how much recent work can be lost. everysec syncs once per second and can lose about one second of writes. Propagated writes are buffered and written in beforeSleep before the client receives the reply, which allows the server to write accumulated log entries together. The other sync policies and the durability effect of the background-save mitigation are not stated.

The request path looks up the command in processCommand and invokes its proc handler through call. It also checks ACL and cluster routing. The command definition's location, how it is built or registered, and which metadata an author must supply are not stated.

The artifact identifies redis.conf as the documented configuration surface and shows examples of directives. The implementation location for adding a configuration parameter and how defaults, runtime mutability, and callbacks are declared are not stated.

The artifact mentions compact hashes that share field names among keys with a common schema. The conversion rules, their implementation locations, and any settings for the compact representations of hashes, sets, sorted sets, and lists are not stated.

The artifact locates the readiness event loop in src/ae.c and shows TCP acceptance in src/socket.c handing a connection to src/networking.c. The plug-in points for a new OS readiness API or a new client transport are not stated.

At maxmemory, Redis tries to evict keys according to maxmemory-policy. The default noeviction policy means writes needing additional memory fail at the limit. They also fail if eviction is enabled but no key can be evicted. The memory categories excluded from accounting and any instance exemptions are not stated.
A failed background snapshot makes Redis stop accepting writes by default so the operator notices. The behavior for a damaged AOF at startup and for an un-loadable data file is not stated.

Replication is asynchronous. An acknowledged write may be lost at failover, and a configured minimum number of replicas does not guarantee that those replicas accept a specific write. The operator can configure the master to refuse writes when too few replicas are available within a configured number of seconds, narrowing the loss window. How a disconnected replica treats client requests is not stated.

Cluster mode partitions keys over 16,384 slots and redirects commands to the node that owns their keys. Multi-key operations require all keys to be in the same slot. Restrictions on logical databases and what happens to availability when some slots have no serving node are not stated.

notes: The overview, command flow diagram, and persistence deep dive made the high-level behavior easy to find. The task index had no routes, so I searched across the artifact for implementation details and failure modes that the narrative often left open.
